summary: Craig Barton's Tips for Teachers summarizes Joseph F. Ciofalo and E. Caroline Wylie's paper on embedding diagnostic multiple-choice items into daily teaching as a formative-assessment tool. The paper argues that while standardized tests reveal broad learning problems, it is classroom-level diagnostic items — used one at a time — that let teachers act on evidence immediately. Diagnostic items are questions whose incorrect answer choices are deliberately built around known student misconceptions, so an incorrect response tells the teacher something specific rather than just wrong. Drawing on work with 4th and 8th grade maths and science teachers, the paper frames formative assessment as a cycle of eliciting evidence and using it right away to adjust instruction — at the start of a lesson to set a baseline, mid-lesson to choose a path, or near the end to catch stragglers. Because the stakes are low, teachers are freed from some of the constraints of high-stakes testing, including the option to write items with more than one correct answer if that generates useful discussion. The tradeoff is that writing genuinely diagnostic distractors — ones tied to real misconceptions rather than arbitrary wrong answers — takes real effort.
points: Diagnostic items work because incorrect answers are engineered around specific misconceptions, so every response (not just the correct one) gives the teacher diagnostic information.
Formative assessment is only formative if the evidence is used immediately — to adjust the current lesson, give feedback, or shape what comes next — not just to log data.
Items can be deployed flexibly within a lesson: as a baseline check at the start, a fork-in-the-road decision mid-lesson, or a check for stragglers near the end.
Low-stakes diagnostic items can break the usual test-writing rules (e.g., allowing two correct answers) if doing so opens up richer classroom discussion.
Writing quality diagnostic items — where distractors map onto real misconceptions — requires significant deliberate effort, not just writing plausible-sounding wrong answers.
quotes: Teachers must use questioning specifically designed to find out not just what students know, but what they do not know. Diagnostic items are powerful because an incorrect response provides specific insight into the nature of the student's misconceptions—inaccurate, incomplete, or partial understandings.

Formative assessment is defined as a process where evidence of learning is evoked and then used immediately to modify the teaching and learning activities. Teachers should use this evidence to adjust instruction as necessary, provide immediate feedback to individuals or the whole class, or structure the next lesson.

Teachers are encouraged to use individual diagnostic items efficiently and flexibly, using just “one item at a time” within the flow of day-to-day lessons. An item can be used at the start of a lesson to determine a baseline understanding, mid-way to decide between instructional paths, or near the end of instruction to identify struggling students.

When developing or selecting diagnostic items, the main concern is ensuring that incorrect answer choices (distractors) are related to common student misconceptions. Because the stakes are very low, teachers are freed from some constraints of high-stakes testing; for example, they can include two correct answers if it generates valuable classroom discussion.

Teachers must ensure they use valid items that specifically uncover misconceptions. Constructing these quality questions, where incorrect choices relate to common student errors, requires a “great deal of effort” and is critical for accurate diagnosis.
